flashcards.definition: The small USB connector once used on smaller peripherals such as early digital cameras; it is rarely used now.
The flatter USB connector used on smaller devices such as smartphones and tablets; its USB 3 version will not plug into a USB 2 port.
The compact, reversible USB connector introduced with USB 3.1; besides data and charging, it can carry video when the port supports DisplayPort or Thunderbolt.
High Speed USB at 480 Mbps, which introduced the Mini and Micro connectors; its cables can run up to 5 meters.
SuperSpeed USB at 5 Gbps, later renamed USB 3.1 Gen 1; its connectors often have a blue tab, and its Type A plugs also fit USB 2 ports.
The most common display type, lit by a backlight (LED in modern panels, fluorescent tubes in older ones); its three main subtypes are IPS, TN, and VA.
An LCD type with crystals aligned parallel to the screen; its superior color accuracy and wide viewing angles suit graphic design, but it responds slower than TN.
An LCD type whose crystals twist 90 degrees; its faster response times and higher refresh rates suit gaming, but it has poorer color and limited viewing angles.
An LCD type with vertically aligned crystals that tilt under voltage; it has better color and viewing angles than TN but slower response, and colors can shift at extreme angles.
A display where each pixel emits its own light, giving true blacks and excellent contrast and color; static images left on too long can cause burn-in.
An LCD enhancement, not a type of OLED, that backlights the screen with thousands of tiny LEDs for better brightness and contrast, but without OLED's true blacks.
Lets a user interact directly with a display by touch or stylus; common in smartphones, tablets, and some laptops.
Converts DC power to AC for the backlight in older LCDs; modern displays with LED backlighting typically do not need one.
How closely a screen's pixels are packed together; higher density results in sharper images.
How often a display redraws its image, measured in hertz (Hz); higher rates give smoother motion for gaming and video playback.
The number of pixels across and down a display, which defines its clarity and detail: Full HD is 1920x1080, Quad HD 2560x1440, and 4K 3840x2160.
The range of colors a display can produce; a wider gamut, such as DCI-P3 compared with sRGB, gives more vibrant and accurate color.
Carries high-definition video and audio through a single cable; the common connection for TVs, monitors, and gaming consoles.
A digital display interface with higher resolutions and refresh rates than HDMI; it also carries audio and can run several monitors from one port with Multi-Stream Transport (MST).
An interface for both displays and peripherals, marked with a lightning bolt icon; versions 3 and 4 use the USB-C connector and run at up to 40 Gbps.
Apple's proprietary, reversible connector for iPhones and iPads; it needs an adapter cable to reach a PC's USB port and is being phased out for USB-C.
The 4-pin PSU connector that powers legacy internal drives and components, usually white or clear plastic, with red 5 VDC, yellow 12 VDC, and black ground wires.
The external version of SATA, with better-shielded cables up to 2 meters long; unlike USB or Thunderbolt, it supplies no power over the cable.
The legacy parallel expansion bus, typically 32-bit at up to 133 MBps, that PCIe replaced; its cards cannot fit into PCIe slots.
The standard form factor for most desktop motherboards and cases; a full-size board measures 12 x 9.6 inches and can have up to seven expansion slots.
A square 9.6 x 9.6 inch motherboard with up to four expansion slots; most of these boards also mount in ATX cases.
A 6.7 x 6.7 inch motherboard with one expansion slot, used in small form factor (SFF) PCs for home use and mini servers; it also fits ATX cases.
A motherboard connector for parts on the case panels, such as the power button, drive activity light, audio ports, and USB ports (9-pin for USB 2, 20-pin for USB 3).
A card that plugs into a PCIe or PCI slot on the motherboard to add functions or ports the motherboard does not already have.
Also called a graphics adapter, it generates the signal for a monitor or projector; a discrete card for 3D gaming or CAD usually goes in a PCIe x16 slot.
Records incoming video, such as gameplay, and saves it as a file or streams it live; internal cards use a PCIe slot, and external ones connect by USB or Thunderbolt.
A PCIe or PCI card for audio playback and microphone recording, with better sound than onboard audio; speakers and headphones plug into its 3.5 mm jacks.
An add-on network card, installed to use a different network type or cabling (copper or fiber optic) or to add ports that can be bonded into one faster link.
An older video-only interface (no audio) that can be analog or digital: DVI-I carries both, DVI-A only analog, and DVI-D only digital.
The legacy 15-pin analog video interface, with a D-shell connector held by screws; it carries no audio and typically supports up to Full HD (1920x1080).
A legacy interface that sends data one bit at a time at up to about 115 Kbps; Windows calls it a COM port, and network equipment may still use it for device management.
The cheaper 9-pin D-subminiature port PCs use for RS-232 serial, in place of the 25-pin interface the standard specifies.
An adapter cable with circuitry that converts the signal itself, such as digital HDMI to analog VGA; needed when the two ends use different protocols.
An adapter cable that changes only the connector type, not the signal, such as USB-C to USB-A; it works when both ends use the same signaling standard.
